and WILLIAM PRICE, VI. ID.

Its title indicates, the journal now offered
to the patronage of the public, will be con-duct-
ed entirely on the principle of Selection. The
leading feature of the plan, as acknowledged
stated, is to present, at stated intervals, a sort of
synopsis of the foreign Magazines, Journals,
and treatises, appropriated to Medicine and
Science.

No one will doubt the importance of this de-
sign, who is conversant with the periodical
works of Europe. As is incident to such pub-
lications, the matter which they contain is al-
together of a mixed nature, and of merit more
unequal. They are a vast field, where golden
wheat is often choked by useless chaff,
and where it imports us like the
prudent husbandman, to reject the one, and
hoard the other. These publications are,
moreover, at this time so numerous, so costly
and so difficult to be procured, that really they
can only be consulted by a small minority of the
cultivators of science in the United States, to
a medium similar to the one now
proposed. It is therefore meant to give an en-
tract so copious of other contents, as not only to
exhibit the progress of the Physical Sciences as
broad, but to do away, in a great degree, the
necessity of recourse to the works themselves.

The contents of the Journal will be arranged
under the division of

I. Selected Papers.

II. Selected Reviews.

III. Medical and Philosophical Intelligence.

IV. List of New Publications.

The work is published in numbers in Janua-
ry, April, July, and October, forming yearly a
volume.

sophical and Medical, which commenced in January,
1821.

Maria Louisa, the widow of Bonaparte. So far as can be judged from external appearances, she is not very deeply affected at the loss of her husband; and even bears the privation of an Imperial diadem philosophically enough. Her venerable relative, King Ferdinand, is making every effort to amuse her, and she enters very readily into all the schemes proposed with that view. I saw his Majesty the other evening driving her in his barouche on the Corso. This is the more remarkable, both because he never paid his Queen that honor and also because it is a rule which he has long observed not to appear on the Corso, at all. On the 11th, the august traveller went to the Royal seat of Parciano, whence she visited the striking ruins of Postum. On the 6th, she went in person through the Albergo di Poveri, and noticed all the arrangements of that institution. The day following she partook of the amusements of the annual festival held at the Royal Villa of Cardinale. Among the cool and tranquil shades of an extensive wood, were assembled from 90 to 1500 peasants in their holiday clothes, disporting and amusing themselves as mirthfully and much more peaceably than you ever saw in Britain. They had arrived from various parts of the surrounding country, and were dressed in the costumes of their respective districts, which afforded great variety of forms, many of them extremely picturesque. On such occasions we see the bright side of absolute monarchy; as in London, a Bullock hunt, or a Munster fair, we behold the barbarous features of liberty.

The King and his Suite arrived at 9 o'clock, and he mounted on horseback, and accompanied the Archduchess of Parma (who had reached the spot with the Duke of Calabria and his sons) in a ride round the woods. Loud and reiterated acclamations rose on all sides.

London Paper.
